title: Relative clauses and connectors
objectives: I can build longer sentences with the relative pronouns que, quem, onde, o que, o qual and cujo.
I can place the right preposition before a relative pronoun and recognize the colloquial version without it.
I can link ideas with connectors of contrast, conclusion, cause and concession, and choose indicative or subjunctive after them and inside relative clauses.
I can write a short, coherent paragraph that states a point, supports it, contrasts it and concludes.
I can explain why the words of this unit are spelled and stressed as they are.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: po-RÉM. An ending in em predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so stress on the last syllable needs a written accent, and Brazilian spelling writes the acute on an e before a final m (também, além). The em is a nasal vowel: the m does not close the lips. Usage: more formal than mas; it can open a clause or sit in the middle, between commas. Its parts are not transparent today, so no word-for-word gloss is given.

example.pt: O apartamento é pequeno, porém bem localizado.
example.en: The apartment is small but well located.

vocabulary.note: Built from com plus tudo, so it once meant with all that. Usage: formal and mostly written; set off by commas. Spelling: con-TU-do. The n only nasalizes the o before it, and the ending o predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent is written.

example.pt: O preço subiu; contudo, as vendas não baixaram.
example.en: The price went up; nevertheless, sales did not drop.
example.literal: The price rose; with-everything, the sales not lowered.

vocabulary.note: Built from entre plus tanto, so it once meant in the meantime. Usage: formal and mostly written, like contudo. Spelling: en-tre-TAN-to. The en and the an are nasal vowels (the n ends its syllable), and the ending o predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent is written.

example.pt: Ela queria ir; entretanto, teve que trabalhar.
example.en: She wanted to go; however, she had to work.
example.literal: She wanted to-go; between-so-much, she-had that to-work.

vocabulary.note: No is em plus o, the contraction from the lesson on contractions. Entanto is entre plus tanto, so the phrase once meant in the meantime. Usage: the standard careful way to say however; a comma follows it. Spelling: en-TAN-to with two nasal vowels.

example.pt: Estudei muito; no entanto, não passei na prova.
example.en: I studied a lot; yet I didn't pass the exam.
example.literal: I-studied much; in-the meanwhile, not I-passed in-the exam.

vocabulary.note: Built from por plus tanto, for so much. Usage: formal; it introduces the result of what was just said, so the result comes second. In speech people say então or por isso. Spelling: por-TAN-to, with the r closing the first syllable and a nasal an.

example.pt: Choveu muito; portanto, o jogo não começou.
example.en: It rained a lot; therefore, the game did not start.
example.literal: It-rained much; for-so-much, the game not began.

vocabulary.note: In most uses logo means soon or right away: Vamos descobrir logo in the third dialogue is we will find out soon. As a connector it introduces a conclusion that follows immediately from the first clause, which is why one word covers both meanings. Usage: formal, often written, with a comma; the classic example is Penso, logo existo. Spelling: LO-go, with a hard g because g before o is hard.

example.pt: Ele não respondeu, logo não quer ir.
example.en: He didn't answer, so he doesn't want to go.
example.literal: He not answered, soon not wants to-go.

vocabulary.note: Followed by a noun or an infinitive, not by a conjugated verb (the longer apesar de que does take one, but it is formal and uncommon); before an article it contracts (apesar do, apesar da). It comes from a plus pesar, to weigh or to grieve, and that sense is no longer felt. Spelling: a-pe-ZAR, because a single s between two vowels is z, and the ending r puts the stress on the last syllable.

example.pt: Apesar do cansaço, ela foi trabalhar.
example.en: Despite the tiredness, she went to work.

vocabulary.note: Followed by the subjunctive, because the clause is granted or hypothetical, not asserted. Mesmo on its own means same or even, so mesmo que is even that. Spelling: MES-mo, divided mes-mo; the s ends the first syllable and, before the voiced m, is said z (or zh in accents that say a syllable-ending s as sh). Que: qu before e gives k, and the u is silent.

example.pt: Mesmo que chova, vamos ao parque.
example.en: Even if it rains, we'll go to the park.
example.literal: Same that it-rain, we-go to-the park.

vocabulary.note: Followed by the indicative. It gives a reason that both speakers already know or can see. Spelling: já is a stressed word of one syllable ending in a, so it takes an accent, and the acute shows an open a (like pé and só).

example.pt: Já que você está aqui, vamos almoçar juntos.
example.en: Since you are here, let's have lunch together.
example.literal: Already that you are here, we-go to-have-lunch together.

vocabulary.note: Visto is the participle of ver, so this is seen that, as in seeing that. Followed by the indicative. Usage: formal, mostly written. Spelling: VIS-to, with the s before t said like English s (or sh in some accents).

example.pt: Visto que o prazo acabou, não podemos aceitar o pedido.
example.en: Given that the deadline has passed, we cannot accept the request.
example.literal: Seen that the deadline ended, not we-can to-accept the request.

vocabulary.note: Followed by the indicative. Usage: formal, mostly written. Vez is one syllable ending in z, so there is no accent.

example.pt: Uma vez que todos concordaram, podemos começar.
example.en: Since everyone agreed, we can begin.
example.literal: One time that all agreed, we-can to-begin.

vocabulary.note: Além is beyond, with the same accent as porém (a-LÉM). Disso is the contraction of de plus isso, like daqui; isso is this, and the ss is a sharp s. Usage: adds a further point in the same direction.

example.pt: O bairro é bonito; além disso, é seguro.
example.en: The neighborhood is beautiful; besides, it is safe.
example.literal: The neighborhood is beautiful; beyond this, is safe.

vocabulary.note: Isso is this and points back at the whole previous clause, so por isso names the cause as a result: for this reason. The result comes second. Spelling: the ss of isso is a sharp s.

example.pt: Estava doente, por isso faltei ao trabalho.
example.en: I was sick, so I missed work.
example.literal: I-was sick, for this I-missed to-the work.

vocabulary.note: Agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner: cujo, cuja, cujos, cujas. No article follows it, because it already contains the link and the article (of whom the). Spelling: CU-jo; c before u is hard, and j is the zh of English measure.

example.pt: Conheço uma mulher cujo filho é piloto.
example.en: I know a woman whose son is a pilot.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: con-se-QUÊN-ci-a. The ending ia is two syllables, so the stress falls on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts and so needs an accent. It is a circumflex because an e before n in the middle of a word is written ê by convention. Here qu is one of the few spellings in which the u is pronounced (kwên), and c before i is s.

example.pt: A falta de chuva teve consequências graves.
example.en: The lack of rain had serious consequences.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: mo-TI-vo, stressed on the second to last syllable because the ending o predicts it. The t before i is said like English ch.

example.pt: Qual é o motivo da sua viagem?
example.en: What is the reason for your trip?

vocabulary.note: An ão word is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde is the only mark; the s between vowels is z. In Chegamos à conclusão de que the que is not a relative pronoun: it opens a clause that says what the conclusion is.

example.pt: Chegamos à conclusão de que o plano era bom.
example.en: We came to the conclusion that the plan was good.
example.literal: We-arrived at-the conclusion of that the plan was good.

vocabulary.note: Opens the first point of an argument; the matching closers are por fim and em conclusão. Spelling: pri-MEI-ro has the diphthong ei; in lugar the g is hard before a.

example.pt: Em primeiro lugar, quero agradecer a todos.
example.en: First of all, I want to thank everyone.

vocabulary.note: Introduces the last point of a list. The m in fim is not a lip sound: it nasalizes the i.

example.pt: Por fim, gostaria de fazer uma sugestão.
example.en: Lastly, I would like to make a suggestion.
example.literal: For end, I-would-like of to-make a suggestion.

vocabulary.note: The district as a place; a vizinhança is the people. Spelling: BAIR-ro, divided bair-ro because rr is always split; ai is a diphthong and rr is the strong r.

example.pt: Moro num bairro onde todo mundo se conhece.
example.en: I live in a neighborhood where everyone knows each other.
example.literal: I-live in-a neighborhood where all world oneself knows.

vocabulary.note: The people who live around you and the community they form; from vizinho, neighbor. Spelling: vi-zi-NHAN-ça. The nh is one sound (ny as in canyon), the an is nasal, and ç is s: without the cedilla, c before a would be k.

example.pt: A vizinhança aqui é muito acolhedora.
example.en: The neighbors here are very welcoming.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: a-pa-RÊN-ci-a, with the same reason for the accent as consequência: the ending ia is two syllables, so the stress is on the third to last syllable. In a aparência the article a and the first a of the noun run together in speech into one slightly longer a, but both are written.

example.pt: A aparência da casa engana: por dentro ela é enorme.
example.en: The house's appearance is deceiving: inside, it is huge.
example.literal: The appearance of-the house deceives: by inside she is enormous.

vocabulary.note: Nouns ending in -dade are feminine, which is why the article is a. Spelling: per-so-na-li-DA-de, stressed on the second to last syllable; the d before the weak final e is said like English j.

example.pt: Ela tem uma personalidade forte, mas é muito gentil.
example.en: She has a strong personality, but she is very kind.

vocabulary.note: Also cozy. Feminine acolhedora; it describes people, places and atmospheres. From acolher, to receive. Spelling: a-co-lhe-DOR; lh is one sound (ly as in million), and the ending r puts the stress on the last syllable.

example.pt: A família me recebeu de um jeito muito acolhedor.
example.en: The family welcomed me in a very warm way.
example.literal: The family me received of a way very welcoming.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: so-ci-Á-vel. The ending l predicts stress on the last syllable, but the stress is on the second to last, so the acute is written (compare impossível). The plural sociáveis keeps the accent; c before i is s.

example.pt: Meu irmão é muito sociável e faz amigos com facilidade.
example.en: My brother is very outgoing and makes friends easily.

dialogues.title: O novo bairro
dialogues.context: Rita has moved to a new neighborhood. Her friend Caio comes by to see the area.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Rita, então esse é o bairro onde você mora agora?
lines.en: Rita, so this is the neighborhood where you live now?

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: É. A rua em que eu moro é tranquila, e a vizinhança é muito acolhedora.
lines.en: Yes. The street I live on is quiet, and the neighbors are very welcoming.
lines.literal: Is. The street in which I live is quiet, and the neighbor-group is very welcoming.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Já conheceu alguém?
lines.en: Have you met anyone yet?
lines.literal: Already you-met someone?

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Conheci a dona Lúcia, uma vizinha cujo filho é professor de música. Ela é a pessoa com quem mais converso.
lines.en: I met Dona Lúcia, a neighbor whose son is a music teacher. She's the person I talk to the most.
lines.literal: I-met the dona Lúcia, a neighbor whose son is teacher of music. She is the person with whom most I-talk.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Que legal! E o mercado de que você falou?
lines.en: How nice! And the market you mentioned?
lines.literal: What cool! And the market of which you spoke?

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Fica na esquina. É o lugar onde compro pão todo dia, mas o preço é um pouco alto.
lines.en: It's on the corner. It's the place where I buy bread every day, but the price is a bit high.
lines.literal: It-stays on-the corner. Is the place where I-buy bread all day, but the price is a little high.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Então, apesar do preço, você gosta.
lines.en: So, despite the price, you like it.
lines.literal: Then, despite of-the price, you like.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Gosto, sim. Além disso, a padaria tem um café que eu adoro.
lines.en: I do. Besides, the bakery has a coffee that I love.
lines.literal: I-like, yes. Beyond this, the bakery has a coffee that I adore.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Já que o bairro é tão bom, vou te visitar no sábado.
lines.en: Since the neighborhood is so good, I'll visit you on Saturday.
lines.literal: Already that the neighborhood is so good, I-go you to-visit on-the Saturday.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Vem mesmo! Vou fazer o bolo de que você gosta.
lines.en: Please do! I'll make the cake you like.
lines.literal: Come indeed! I-go to-make the cake of which you like.

dialogues.title: Trabalho remoto: prós e contras
dialogues.context: Vanessa and Otávio discuss an article about remote work and try to reach a reasoned conclusion.

lines.speaker: Vanessa
lines.pt: Otávio, li um artigo sobre trabalho remoto. Em primeiro lugar, ele diz que a produtividade aumenta.
lines.en: Otávio, I read an article about remote work. First of all, it says that productivity increases.
lines.literal: Otávio, I-read an article about work remote. In first place, it says that the productivity increases.

lines.speaker: Otávio
lines.pt: Pode ser, porém eu sinto que perco o contato com a equipe.
lines.en: Maybe, but I feel that I lose contact with the team.
lines.literal: Can be, however I feel that I lose the contact with the team.

lines.speaker: Vanessa
lines.pt: Entendo. No entanto, muita gente economiza tempo, visto que não precisa pegar trânsito.
lines.en: I understand. Yet many people save time, given that they don't have to sit in traffic.
lines.literal: I-understand. In-the meanwhile, much people saves time, seen that not needs to-catch traffic.

lines.speaker: Otávio
lines.pt: Isso é verdade. Mas, mesmo que a gente economize tempo, o isolamento é um problema.
lines.en: That's true. But even if we save time, isolation is a problem.
lines.literal: This is truth. But, same that the people save time, the isolation is a problem.

lines.speaker: Vanessa
lines.pt: Concordo. Por isso, muitas empresas adotam o modelo híbrido.
lines.en: I agree. That's why many companies adopt the hybrid model.
lines.literal: I-agree. For this, many companies adopt the model hybrid.

lines.speaker: Otávio
lines.pt: Faz sentido. Embora eu goste de ficar em casa, prefiro ir ao escritório duas vezes por semana.
lines.en: Makes sense. Although I like staying home, I prefer going to the office twice a week.
lines.literal: It-makes sense. Although I like of to-stay in house, I-prefer to-go to-the office two times per week.

lines.speaker: Vanessa
lines.pt: Então, em resumo, a solução está no meio-termo.
lines.en: So, in short, the solution is the middle ground.
lines.literal: Then, in summary, the solution is in-the middle-term.

lines.speaker: Otávio
lines.pt: Exatamente. Portanto, vou propor isso ao meu chefe.
lines.en: Exactly. Therefore, I'll suggest that to my boss.
lines.literal: Exactly. For-so-much, I-go to-propose this to-the my boss.

lines.speaker: Vanessa
lines.pt: Boa ideia! Já que você vai falar com ele, peça também um horário flexível.
lines.en: Good idea! Since you're going to talk to him, ask for flexible hours too.
lines.literal: Good idea! Already that you go to-speak with him, ask also a schedule flexible.

dialogues.title: Como é o novo gerente?
dialogues.context: Matheus asks his colleague Larissa about the company's new manager.

lines.speaker: Matheus
lines.pt: Larissa, como é o novo gerente de quem todo mundo fala?
lines.en: Larissa, what is the new manager everyone's talking about like?
lines.literal: Larissa, how is the new manager of whom all world speaks?

lines.speaker: Larissa
lines.pt: O Paulo? É um homem alto, de cabelo grisalho, cuja aparência engana. Parece sério, mas é muito simpático.
lines.en: Paulo? He's a tall man with gray hair whose appearance is deceiving. He seems serious, but he's very friendly.
lines.literal: The Paulo? Is a man tall, of hair gray, whose appearance deceives. Seems serious, but is very friendly.

lines.speaker: Matheus
lines.pt: E a personalidade dele?
lines.en: And his personality?
lines.literal: And the personality of-him?

lines.speaker: Larissa
lines.pt: Bem sociável. É o tipo de pessoa que fala com todo mundo, inclusive com quem acabou de chegar.
lines.en: Very outgoing. He's the type of person who talks to everyone, even to someone who has just arrived.
lines.literal: Well sociable. Is the type of person that speaks with all world, including with who finished of to-arrive.

lines.speaker: Matheus
lines.pt: Que bom. O gerente anterior, que era muito reservado, quase não falava com a equipe.
lines.en: Great. The previous manager, who was very reserved, hardly ever talked to the team.
lines.literal: What good. The manager previous, who was very reserved, almost not spoke with the team.

lines.speaker: Larissa
lines.pt: Pois é. O Paulo conhece bem o setor, o que facilita o trabalho dele.
lines.en: Exactly. Paulo knows the sector well, which makes his job easier.
lines.literal: Well is. The Paulo knows well the sector, the which makes-easier the work of-him.

lines.speaker: Matheus
lines.pt: Ele já fez alguma mudança?
lines.en: Has he made any changes yet?
lines.literal: He already made some change?

lines.speaker: Larissa
lines.pt: Já. Marcou uma reunião semanal, o que a equipe adorou.
lines.en: Yes. He scheduled a weekly meeting, which the team loved.
lines.literal: Already. He-scheduled a meeting weekly, the which the team loved.

lines.speaker: Matheus
lines.pt: Entretanto, ainda não sei como ele reage a críticas.
lines.en: However, I still don't know how he reacts to criticism.
lines.literal: Between-so-much, still not I-know how he reacts to criticisms.

lines.speaker: Larissa
lines.pt: Vamos descobrir logo, já que a avaliação do projeto é na sexta.
lines.en: We'll find out soon, since the project review is on Friday.
lines.literal: We-go to-discover soon, already that the evaluation of-the project is on-the Friday.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the connectors and the new vocabulary
grammar.explanation:
No word in this unit needs a new rule. Every spelling follows the method of the first three lessons: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable, read the default for the ending, and compare. A written accent appears only when the stress breaks the default of the ending, and its shape, acute or circumflex, says whether the vowel is open or closed. This note applies the method to the connectors and the other new vocabulary, in four families. The next note does the same for the words of the dialogues and the reading.

Family one: last-syllable stress in a word ending in em. The default for an ending in em is the second to last syllable (HO-mem), so a word stressed on its last syllable needs an accent. Porém (po-RÉM) and além (a-LÉM) are exactly that, and Brazilian spelling writes the acute on an e before a final m, as in também. The vowel is nasal: the m only nasalizes it, so the lips never close. Já is the same logic in a smaller word. A stressed word of one syllable that ends in a, e or o takes an accent (pé, só, já), and the acute shows an open a, like the a in father.

Family two: nasal vowels inside a word. In contudo, entretanto, entanto and portanto, an n sits before a consonant and ends its syllable. It is not a consonant sound there. It only nasalizes the vowel before it: con-TU-do, en-tre-TAN-to, por-TAN-to. All of these words end in o, so the default is stress on the second to last syllable (tu, tan, tan), and no accent is needed. The r in por closes its syllable and is also not a separate beat.

Family three: the endings ia and io. In consequência and aparência the final i and a count as two syllables for the purpose of stress: con-se-QUÊN-ci-a. The stressed syllable is therefore the third to last, which no ending predicts, so it must carry an accent, exactly as in salário and negócio. The accent is a circumflex because a stressed e, o or a before n or m in the middle of a word is written with a circumflex by convention (compare acadêmico, Antônio and câmera in the lesson on accents). Two more letters appear there: c before i is s, and the qu of consequência is one of the few spellings in which the u is pronounced (kwên, as in cinquenta and tranquilo).

Family four: adjectives in -ável. In sociável (so-ci-Á-vel) the ending l predicts stress on the last syllable, but the stress is on the second to last, so the acute is written, as in impossível. The plural sociáveis keeps the accent.

The consonant letters follow the lesson on sounds. A single s between vowels is z (apesar, causa, conclusão), while ss is a sharp s (isso, disso). The ç is s before a, o or u and exists because plain c there would be k (vizinhança). The digraphs nh and lh are single sounds (vizinhança, acolhedor), rr is the strong r (bairro), and t and d before an i sound are like English ch and j (motivo, personalidade, whose d is followed by a weak final e). The j of cujo is the zh of measure, and c and g are hard before a, o and u.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of the dialogues and the reading
grammar.explanation:
The dialogues and the reading use many words beyond the vocabulary list. None needs a rule you have not met, so this note goes through the ones whose spelling could still puzzle you, grouped by the question they answer. The aim is that each spelling is a conclusion from a rule, never a fact to memorize.

Where does the stress fall, and does it need an accent? An ending in ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so these words carry only the tilde: então, solução, reunião, avaliação. A word stressed on the third to last syllable always needs an accent, because no ending predicts that position: música, sábado, trânsito, híbrido, crítica, simpático. Words ending in ia or io belong here too, since the i and the vowel after it are two syllables: Lúcia, família, Otávio, escritório, horário. The vowel quality decides the mark: an open a, e or o takes the acute (sábado, escritório), a closed e or o takes the circumflex (pêssego, ônibus), a before n or m in the middle of a word takes the circumflex by convention (trânsito), and i and u, which have only one quality, take the acute (música, híbrido). A word ending in l takes an accent when the stress is not on the last syllable: flexível.

Which letters are silent, or change their sound? In que, qui, gue and gui the u is silent (equipe, esquina), and in a few words it is sounded (tranquila). The letter x has several values and the word decides: z between vowels in exatamente and existe, s before a consonant in sexta, ks in flexível. The group sc before e or i writes a single s sound (nasci, from nascer). The letter g before e or i is zh (viagem, gerente). The letter h at the start of a word is silent (hoje), and t before i, including the i that a final e becomes, is ch (simpático, Tiradentes).

Which vowels form a diphthong, and which do not? A diphthong is two vowel letters that glide into one beat (pai, bairro, deixei). A hiatus is two vowels that are separate beats. In atraem, the a and the e are separate, and no accent is written because the ending em already puts the stress on the second to last syllable. In raízes, the stressed i follows an a and ends its own syllable, so the accent is written to show that ai is not read as a diphthong (without it, the word would be read RAI-zes); this is the same accent as in país and saúde. In the singular raiz, the final z closes the syllable, so no accent is needed.

grammar.title: Relative clauses: que, quem, onde, o que, o qual and cujo
grammar.explanation:
A clause is a group of words with its own verb. A sentence can hold more than one clause: a main clause, which could stand alone (Conheço uma mulher), and a dependent clause, which hangs on another and cannot stand alone (que mora aqui). A relative clause is a dependent clause that describes a noun of the main clause. That noun is called the antecedent, because it comes before the pronoun that points back at it, and the pronoun that opens the relative clause is a relative pronoun. It does two jobs at once: it joins the clause to the antecedent, and it stands in for the antecedent inside the clause, so the noun is not said twice. Start from two sentences, O filme era ótimo and Nós vimos o filme ontem. In the second, o filme becomes que and moves to the front of its clause, and the clause is placed right after the noun it describes: O filme que vimos ontem era ótimo.

English chooses among who, whom, which, that, whose and where, and it may drop the pronoun when it is the object (the movie we saw). Portuguese may never drop it: que is always written. In return, que does the work of most of the English words. It refers to people and things, and it can be the subject (a moça que mora aqui, the girl who lives here) or the object (o livro que li, the book I read). It never changes form. The other relative pronouns exist for specific situations: a person after a preposition, a place, a whole idea, an antecedent whose gender must be made clear, and possession.

Quem means who and refers only to people. It is used after a preposition (a pessoa com quem falei) and, with no antecedent at all, as the one who (Quem chegar primeiro escolhe, from the lesson on the future subjunctive). It does not change for gender or number. Onde means where and refers to a place: a cidade onde nasci is the same as a cidade em que nasci. Onde is only for places; for a moment or a situation use em que (o dia em que nos conhecemos).

O que has no noun antecedent. Its o is not an article before a noun but a pronoun meaning that thing (compare aquilo), so o que is that which, and it refers back to a whole idea. In Ela passou no concurso, o que deixou todos felizes, what made everyone happy was not a noun but the fact that she passed. Set off by a comma, it comments on the previous clause. Without any antecedent it means what: Não entendi o que você disse, Tudo o que ele disse é verdade.

O qual is qual (which) plus an article, and it agrees with its antecedent: o qual, a qual, os quais, as quais (the plural follows the rule that a final l becomes is). Because it shows gender and number, it removes an ambiguity that que cannot. In O diretor da empresa, o qual viajou ontem, ligou, the masculine o qual shows that it is the director who traveled, not the company. It is formal and written, usually after a comma or after a preposition (next note).

Cujo means whose. It replaces of whom plus the article of the thing owned, so a mulher cujo filho é piloto is word for word the woman of-whom the son is pilot. That explains two facts. No article follows cujo, because it already contains one. And it agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: cujo filho, cuja filha, cujos filhos, cujas filhas, even when the owner is feminine. English whose never changes. In speech Brazilians rarely say cujo. They say a mulher que o filho dela é piloto, where que supplies the link and dela repeats the owner, and that version is not accepted in formal writing.

Finally, a relative clause can identify which one is meant, or it can add information about a noun that is already identified. Os alunos que estudaram passaram says that only the students who studied passed. Os alunos, que estudaram, passaram says that all passed, and they had studied. The commas carry the difference, as in English.

grammar.title: Prepositions before relatives, and the colloquial version
grammar.explanation:
Many verbs require a particular preposition before their object: gostar de, falar com, morar em, precisar de, sonhar com, trabalhar para. The preposition belongs to the verb, and you learn it with the verb. When the object of such a verb turns into a relative pronoun, the preposition does not disappear. It must stand immediately before the pronoun. Build it in steps. From O livro é esse and Eu preciso do livro (precisar de), replace o livro by que, keep de in front of it, and move the whole group to the front of its clause: O livro de que preciso é esse.

English handles this differently in two ways, and both cause mistakes. English may leave the preposition at the end (the person I spoke with), which Portuguese never does: a pessoa que falei com is impossible, and the standard order is a pessoa com quem falei. And English may show no preposition at all where Portuguese needs one: the book I need, but o livro de que preciso. So check the Portuguese verb, not the English sentence.

Which pronoun follows the preposition? For people, quem: com quem, de quem, para quem. For things, que after a short preposition (a, com, de, em, por): a cidade em que moro, o livro de que preciso. After a longer preposition (sobre, durante, contra, entre, para when a thing follows) and whenever gender and number must be clear, o qual, a qual, os quais, as quais: o assunto sobre o qual falamos, o período durante o qual. The preposition contracts with the article inside o qual, as it does anywhere: por plus a qual is pela qual (a razão pela qual), em plus o qual is no qual, de plus os quais is dos quais, and a plus a qual is à qual, with the crase of the lesson on contractions. Para does not contract: a empresa para a qual trabalho.

In casual speech, Brazilians very often drop the preposition and keep only que: o lugar que eu gosto, a pessoa que eu falei, o livro que eu preciso, o emprego que eu sonho. This works because que needs no agreement and no preposition, so it is the easiest thing to say, and everyone understands it. A second spoken pattern repeats the noun as a pronoun after the verb: a pessoa que eu falei com ela. Neither is accepted in exams, reports or official documents, where the standard form is expected. Learn to recognize both in listening and use the standard form in writing.

For places, onde is the easy option: a casa onde cresci equals a casa em que cresci. With a verb of movement the preposition a joins it, giving aonde (a cidade aonde vou), although in speech people simply say onde. Do not use onde for times or situations, where the standard form is em que: o dia em que nos conhecemos, not o dia onde.

grammar.title: Connectors: contrast, conclusion, cause, concession and addition
grammar.explanation:
A connector is a word or phrase whose only job is to say how one statement relates to another. Choosing the connector is choosing the logic: but, so, because, although and besides each assert a different relation between the same two facts. Three questions decide the choice. What relation is meant (contrast, result, cause, concession, addition, order)? What register is right, everyday or formal? And what follows: a whole clause, a noun or an infinitive, and in which mood?

There are two kinds. Some are conjunctions that join two clauses into one sentence: mas, porque, já que, embora, mesmo que. Others are linking words that open a new clause, often after a semicolon or a period, and link it to what came before (English grammar calls these conjunctive adverbs: however, therefore): porém, contudo, entretanto, no entanto, portanto, por isso, além disso. A comma follows them, and some can move inside the clause: O plano é bom, porém arriscado, or O plano, porém, é arriscado. English has the same two kinds (but against however).

Contrast. Mas is the everyday word and is never wrong. Porém, contudo, entretanto, no entanto and todavia are formal equivalents, used in writing to avoid repeating mas. Conclusion and cause point in opposite directions, and the common mistake is to pick the word for the wrong direction. Portanto, logo, por isso, então and assim introduce the result, and the result comes second: Choveu; portanto, ficamos em casa. Porque, já que, visto que, uma vez que and pois, and como at the start of a sentence, introduce the reason: the clause they open is the cause, whether it comes second (Ficamos em casa já que choveu) or first (Já que choveu, ficamos em casa). Já que suits a reason both speakers already know; visto que and uma vez que are formal and mostly written. All the reason connectors take the indicative, since a reason is given as true.

Concession admits something and then says it does not change the main point. Apesar de is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an infinitive, not by a conjugated verb (the longer apesar de que does take one, but it is formal and uncommon): Apesar da chuva, saímos; Apesar de estar doente, ele trabalhou. The infinitive version needs the same subject in both parts. When the subjects differ, use embora or mesmo que, both followed by the subjunctive: Embora ele esteja doente, nós vamos. The difference between them is that embora grants something true (although it is), while mesmo que treats the clause as a hypothesis (even if it is).

Addition and order. Além disso adds a further point in the same direction, and ademais is its formal equivalent. To structure a longer argument, open with em primeiro lugar, continue with em segundo lugar or além disso, and close with por fim or em conclusão. One connector per logical step is enough; a paragraph that piles them up reads as heavy.

grammar.title: Review: indicative or subjunctive after connectors and inside relative clauses
grammar.explanation:
The verb of a dependent clause shows the speaker's stance toward what the clause says. The indicative presents it as a fact, known or taken as true. The subjunctive presents it as something that is not being asserted: a purpose, a hypothesis, something still to come, or a fact that is only granted. The connector usually fixes the stance, so you learn the mood together with the connector, in groups.

Reasons are facts: porque, já que, visto que, uma vez que, pois and como at the start of a sentence take the indicative. Concession is granted, not asserted: embora and mesmo que take the subjunctive. Purpose, condition and a time that has not arrived take the subjunctive: para que, sem que, antes que, caso, a menos que, contanto que. Time words and se follow the time frame: with a past event or a habit, the indicative (Quando cheguei, Sempre que chove); with a future event, the future subjunctive (Quando eu chegar, Se você quiser). An unreal condition uses se plus the imperfect subjunctive, with the conditional in the main clause (Se eu tivesse tempo, viajaria). Apesar de takes no mood because it is a preposition and is followed by a noun or an infinitive, never by a conjugated verb.

The tense of the subjunctive follows the main clause. With a present or future main clause, the dependent verb is in the present subjunctive: Mesmo que chova, vamos. With a past or conditional main clause, it moves to the imperfect subjunctive: Mesmo que chovesse, iríamos (even if it rained, we would go); Saí antes que chovesse. This is the same shift English makes between even if it rains, we go and even if it rained, we would go.

A relative clause follows the same logic. If the antecedent is a real, identified person or thing, the clause states a fact and takes the indicative: Conheço um médico que fala alemão. If the antecedent is sought, wanted or does not exist, the clause describes something not yet established, and the verb is in the subjunctive: Procuro um médico que fale alemão; Não há ninguém que saiba a resposta. English says who speaks in both cases, so the listener cannot tell whether you have a particular doctor in mind; Portuguese tells them through the verb.

A short checklist: does the sentence present the clause as a fact? Indicative. Does it express a purpose, a doubt, a wish, a hypothesis, a possible future, or something merely granted? Subjunctive. If you are unsure, ask what the speaker takes to be true at the moment of speaking.

culture.title: The written argument and the Enem essay
culture.text:
In Brazil, writing a well-structured argument is a skill that students practice intensely, because the national exam Enem, used to enter universities, includes a redação: a dissertative-argumentative essay with an introduction, two development paragraphs and a conclusion that proposes a solution. Graders look for the correct use of connectors such as portanto, além disso, no entanto and diante disso (literally before this). Students learn these words by heart, which is why they are a reliable sign of formal written Portuguese.

In conversation, the rules relax. Instead of entretanto or contudo, Brazilians simply say mas, and instead of cujo they rearrange the sentence. The preposition before que is often dropped: o lugar que eu gosto, a pessoa que eu falei. This spoken version is universally understood and is not treated as a sign of ignorance in casual contexts, but you should avoid it in exams, reports and cover letters. The difference is a difference of register, not of correctness in the everyday sense: the same speaker uses the standard form on paper and the shortened one at the dinner table.

Describing people and places in detail is also a social skill. Brazilians often praise a place as acolhedor (welcoming, from acolher, to receive) or a person as sociável, and typical descriptions use que and onde to add detail: um bairro onde todo mundo se conhece, uma pessoa que faz amigos em qualquer lugar.

exercises.prompt: Mesmo que chovesse, nós ___ ao parque.
exercises.explanation: A past subjunctive (chovesse) goes with a conditional main clause: even if it rained, we would go.

exercises.prompt: Já que você ___ aqui, vamos almoçar.
exercises.explanation: Já que gives a reason as a fact, so it takes the indicative.

exercises.prompt: Quero uma casa que ___ um jardim grande.
exercises.explanation: The house is wanted but not yet identified, so the relative clause is not a fact and takes the subjunctive.

exercises.prompt_pt: Não há ninguém que ___ a resposta.
exercises.hint_en: There is nobody who knows the answer.
exercises.explanation: A relative clause whose antecedent does not exist takes the subjunctive; saiba is the present subjunctive of saber.

exercises.prompt: In dialogue 3, Larissa says 'Vamos descobrir logo'. What does logo mean there?
exercises.explanation: Logo means soon in most uses. It means therefore only when it joins two clauses and introduces a conclusion.

exercises.prompt: Why does porém carry a written accent?
choices: It distinguishes it from a plural
It is stressed on the last syllable, and an ending in em predicts the second to last
exercises.explanation: Words ending in em default to stress on the second to last syllable. Stress on the last syllable breaks that default, so the stressed e takes an acute, as in também.

exercises.prompt: Why does aparência have an accent?
choices: The ending ia is two syllables, so the stress is on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts
The ending ia is a nasal diphthong
An accent is needed on any word with c before i
exercises.explanation: Stress on the third to last syllable always needs an accent. The circumflex is the convention for an e before n in the middle of a word.

exercises.prompt: Why is vizinhança written with ç and not with c?
choices: Without the cedilla, c before a would sound like k
The cedilla marks the stressed syllable
The cedilla marks a nasal vowel
exercises.explanation: Before a, o and u, c is a k sound. The ç keeps the s sound.

exercises.audio_pt: Apesar do calor, fomos à praia.
choices: Because of the heat, we stayed home.
Despite the heat, we went to the beach.
Since it was hot, we went to the pool.

exercises.audio_pt: Mesmo que chova, vamos ao parque.
choices: Because it rains, we go to the park.
If it doesn't rain, we'll go to the park.
Even if it rains, we'll go to the park.

exercises.audio_pt: Procuro um médico que fale alemão.
choices: I'm looking for a doctor who speaks German.
I know a doctor who speaks German.
I'm looking for a doctor who speaks English.

exercises.audio_pt: A pessoa com quem mais converso é minha vizinha.
exercises.hint_en: The person I talk to the most is my neighbor.

exercises.audio_pt: Em primeiro lugar, quero agradecer a todos.
exercises.hint_en: First of all, I want to thank everyone.

exercises.audio_pt: O apartamento é pequeno, porém bem localizado.
exercises.hint_en: The apartment is small but well located.

exercises.prompt: Match each connector with its function

exercises.prompt_en: I know a woman whose son is a pilot.
answers: Conheço uma mulher cujo filho é piloto.
Eu conheço uma mulher cujo filho é piloto.

exercises.prompt_en: The city where I live is big.
answers: A cidade onde moro é grande.
A cidade onde eu moro é grande.
A cidade em que moro é grande.
A cidade em que eu moro é grande.
A cidade na qual moro é grande.
A cidade na qual eu moro é grande.
A cidade que eu moro é grande.

exercises.prompt_en: The book I need is here. (Use the standard written form.)
answers: O livro de que preciso está aqui.
O livro de que eu preciso está aqui.
O livro do qual preciso está aqui.
O livro do qual eu preciso está aqui.

exercises.prompt_en: Despite the rain, we went out.
answers: Apesar da chuva, a gente saiu.
A gente saiu apesar da chuva.
